name: Reading an error
front: What do you do when the code will not run?
what: When Godot cannot run your code it stops and shows an error: the line number and what it expected to find there.
how:
Parse Error: Expected closing ")" after function call
   at: line 2
example: Line 2 is `print("Hello"` — the closing bracket is missing, so you add it.
mistake: Reading only the first word of the error. The line number and the words after "expected" tell you exactly where to look.

name: Pairs that must close
front: Which characters always come in pairs?
what: Brackets `( )`, square brackets `[ ]` and quotes `" "` come in pairs. Every opening one needs its closing one on the same line.
example: `print("Hi")` has one pair of brackets and one pair of quotes.
mistake: Closing the quote but forgetting the bracket: `print("Hi"`.

name: Indentation
front: Why does GDScript care about the spaces at the start of a line?
what: The lines inside a function are pushed in by one tab. That tab is how GDScript knows which lines belong to the function.
example: A line with no tab after `func run():` is an error: the function has an empty body.
mistake: Mixing a tab on one line and spaces on the next. Use the Tab key every time.

name: Calling a built-in function
front: How do you use a function that Godot already provides?
what: Godot comes with functions written by other people. You call one by writing its name followed by brackets.
example: `hide()` hides the robot; you did not have to write how hiding works.
mistake: Leaving out the brackets: `show` on its own does nothing.

name: Argument
front: What goes inside the brackets of a call?
what: An argument is a value you hand to a function inside its brackets. Some functions need one, some need none.
example: `rotate(45)` turns by 45 degrees; the number `45` is the argument.
mistake: Calling `rotate()` with nothing inside when it needs a number.

name: Turtle commands
front: How do you draw a shape with move and turn commands?
what: The turtle draws while it moves. `move_forward` draws a line of a given length; `turn_left` and `turn_right` change the direction by 90 degrees unless you pass another angle.
example: Four `move_forward(80)` calls with `turn_left()` between them draw a square.
mistake: Turning by the wrong angle. A square needs 90 degrees at each corner, a triangle 120.

name: Order of commands
front: Does it matter which line comes first?
what: Code runs from the top line to the bottom, one command at a time. Swapping two lines changes what is drawn.
example: Turning before moving draws a different line than moving before turning.
mistake: Writing the commands in the order you thought of them instead of the order they must happen.

name: Function
front: How do you define your own function?
what: A function is a named block of code you can run by calling its name. `func` starts it, the name and brackets follow, then a colon, then the indented body.
example: `say_hello()` anywhere in the script prints Hello.
mistake: Forgetting the colon at the end of the `func` line, or the tab on the next one.

name: Calling your own function
front: How do you run a function you wrote?
what: Write its name with brackets. Defining a function does nothing on its own; the body only runs when the function is called.
example: Calling `say_hello()` twice prints Hello twice.
mistake: Defining the function and never calling it, then wondering why nothing printed.

name: Parameter
front: How does a function receive a value?
what: A parameter is a name inside the brackets of a `func` line. Each call fills it with the argument you pass, and the body uses it like a variable.
example: `greet("Robo")` prints Hello Robo; inside the function `name` is "Robo".
mistake: Using a different name in the body than the one in the brackets.

name: Argument and parameter
front: What is the difference between an argument and a parameter?
what: The parameter is the name in the definition; the argument is the value in the call. One definition can be called with many different arguments.
how:
func heal(amount):   # amount is the parameter
	health += amount

heal(10)   # 10 is the argument
example: `heal(10)` and `heal(25)` both use the same function with a different `amount`.
mistake: Writing the value in the definition: `func heal(10):` is an error.

name: Member variable
front: How do you make a value that every function in the script can use?
what: A variable declared at the top of the script, outside any function, is a member variable. Every function can read it and change it, and it keeps its value between calls.
example: After `take_damage(30)`, `health` is 70 for the whole script.
mistake: Declaring `var health = 100` inside a function: then it is created fresh on every call and the change is lost.

name: Changing a member from a function
front: How does a function change a value that lives at the top of the script?
what: Just assign to it. No `var` inside the function: `var` would create a new, separate variable.
example: Two calls to `level_up()` leave `level` at 3.
mistake: Writing `var level = level + 1` inside the function, which makes a new local `level` instead of changing the member.

name: Variable
front: How do you make a variable?
what: A variable is a named box for a value. `var` creates it, the name comes next, and `=` puts the first value in.
example: `var speed = 120` makes a variable called speed holding 120.
mistake: Writing `var` every time you use the variable. `var` is only for creating it.

name: Assignment
front: How do you change what a variable holds?
what: `=` puts a new value into an existing variable. The old value is gone. The right side is worked out first, then stored.
example: After `health = health - 20` the variable holds 60.
mistake: Reading `=` as "equals" from maths. It means "store this on the left".

name: Using a variable's value
front: How do you use a variable in a calculation?
what: Write its name where you would write the value. The current value is used at that moment.
how:
var width = 40
var area = width * width
example: `print(health)` prints whatever health holds right now.
mistake: Putting the name in quotes: `print("health")` prints the word, not the number.

name: += and -=
front: What does `health -= 20` mean?
what: `+=` adds to a variable in place and `-=` takes away. `x += 5` is a short way to write `x = x + 5`.
example: With health at 100, `health -= 20` leaves 80.
mistake: Writing `health =- 20`: that stores minus 20.

name: Adding and subtracting
front: How do you add or subtract numbers in code?
what: `+` adds and `-` subtracts, on numbers and on variables holding numbers. The result can be stored, printed or returned.
example: `return health - damage` gives the health after a hit.
mistake: Forgetting to store the result: `health - 20` on its own line changes nothing.

name: _process(delta)
front: Which function runs every frame?
what: Godot calls `_process(delta)` once per frame, many times a second, for as long as the game runs. Anything that should happen continuously goes in it.
example: The robot keeps turning because `turn_right(1)` runs again every frame.
mistake: Calling `_process` yourself. Godot calls it; you only write it.

name: Frame
front: What is a frame?
what: One redraw of the screen. A game draws about 60 frames a second, and between frames it runs your code once.
example: Adding 1 to a variable every frame adds about 60 every second.
mistake: Assuming frames are always exactly a sixtieth of a second: they are not, which is what delta is for.

name: delta
front: What is delta?
what: `delta` is the time the last frame took, in seconds, about 0.016 at 60 frames a second. Godot passes it into `_process` so your code can move by time instead of by frame.
how:
func _process(delta):
	x += 120 * delta   # 120 pixels per second
example: At 30 frames a second delta is about 0.033: fewer, bigger steps, same distance per second.
mistake: Adding a fixed amount per frame: then the game runs faster on a faster computer.

name: Speed times delta
front: How do you move at a steady speed?
what: Multiply a speed in units per second by delta. The result is how far to move this frame, and over a second the frames add up to exactly the speed.
example: With speed 200, one second of frames moves x by 200 whatever the frame rate.
mistake: Multiplying by delta twice, or dividing by it.

name: Named value
front: Why give a number a name?
what: A number on its own, like `250`, tells nobody what it is. A named value like `SPEED` explains itself and is written once, so changing it changes every use.
example: `MAX_HEALTH` in three places beats the number `100` in three places.
mistake: Naming it and then still typing the raw number elsewhere.

name: const
front: What is the difference between const and var?
what: `const` makes a value that never changes; trying to assign to it is an error. Names of constants are written in capitals by convention.
example: `MAX_HEALTH` stays 100 forever; `health` can go up and down.
mistake: Using `const` for something that must change, like the current health.

name: if
front: How do you run code only when something is true?
what: `if` checks a condition. When it is true the indented lines under it run; when it is false they are skipped.
example: With health at 0 the message prints; with health at 50 nothing happens.
mistake: Forgetting the colon after the condition, or not indenting the lines that belong to the if.

name: else
front: How do you run something when the condition is false?
what: `else` follows an `if` and runs its lines only when the `if` condition was false. Exactly one of the two blocks runs.
example: One of Alive or Down prints, never both.
mistake: Writing a condition after `else`. `else` takes no condition; that is what `elif` is for.

name: elif
front: How do you check several conditions in turn?
what: `elif` means "else if". Conditions are checked from the top; the first true one runs its block and the rest are skipped.
example: Health 50 prints Hurt: the first check fails, the second passes.
mistake: Putting the wider condition first, so the narrower one below can never be reached.

name: Comparison operators
front: How do you compare two values?
what: `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<` less, `>` greater, `<=` at most, `>=` at least. Each gives true or false.
example: `health <= 0` is true for 0 and for negative numbers.
mistake: Using one `=` to compare. One `=` assigns; two `==` compare.

name: and, or, not
front: How do you combine two conditions?
what: `and` is true only when both sides are true; `or` when at least one is; `not` flips true and false.
example: `health > 0 or shield > 0` is true when either is above zero.
mistake: Writing `health > 0 and < 100`. Each side needs the full comparison: `health > 0 and health < 100`.

name: true and false
front: What kind of value does a condition give?
what: A bool: either `true` or `false`. Comparisons produce bools, variables can hold them, and `if` reads them.
example: `var is_charged = true` and later `if is_charged:`.
mistake: Writing `if is_alive == true:`. `if is_alive:` already means the same.

name: Multiply and divide
front: How do you multiply or divide?
what: `*` multiplies and `/` divides. They happen before `+` and `-` in the same line, and brackets change the order.
how:
var double = health * 2
var half = health / 2
var total = (a + b) * 2
example: `damage * 3` triples the damage.
mistake: Expecting `2 + 3 * 4` to be 20. It is 14, because multiplying comes first.

name: Dividing whole numbers
front: Why does 7 / 2 give 3?
what: Dividing two whole numbers (ints) gives a whole number: the decimal part is dropped. Make one side a decimal (a float) to keep it.
example: `health / 2` with health 75 gives 37; `health / 2.0` gives 37.5.
mistake: Dividing by an int and losing the half without noticing.

name: Vector2
front: How do you store a position with an x and a y?
what: A Vector2 holds two numbers, `x` and `y`. It is how Godot stores positions, sizes and directions in 2D.
example: `Vector2(0, 0)` is the top-left corner; `Vector2(100, 50)` is 100 right and 50 down.
mistake: Writing `Vector2(10 20)` without the comma, or reading `.y` when you meant `.x`.

name: Vector2 arithmetic
front: How do you move a Vector2?
what: Adding two vectors adds their x values and their y values. Multiplying by a number scales both.
example: `position += direction * speed * delta` moves a character each frame.
mistake: Adding a plain number to a vector: `pos + 5` is an error.

name: Rect2
front: How do you describe a rectangle?
what: A Rect2 holds a `position` (its top-left corner, a Vector2) and a `size` (width and height, a Vector2).
example: `Rect2(10, 10, 20, 20)` is a 20 by 20 square whose corner is at (10, 10).
mistake: Reading the last two numbers as the far corner. They are the width and the height.

name: position and size
front: How do you read a rectangle's width?
what: `rect.size.x` is the width and `rect.size.y` the height; `rect.position` is the top-left corner. The far corner is `rect.position + rect.size`.
how:
var area = box.size.x * box.size.y
var corner = box.position + box.size
example: A rect at (10, 10) with size (20, 30) ends at (30, 40).
mistake: Using `box.x` — a Rect2 has no `x` of its own; it is inside `position`.

name: while loop
front: How do you repeat code until something changes?
what: `while` checks its condition; when true it runs the block, then checks again. It stops the first time the condition is false.
how:
var count = 0
while count < 3:
	print(count)
	count += 1
example: This prints 0, 1, 2 and then stops because count is 3.
mistake: Never changing the variable in the condition: the loop runs forever.

name: The loop must move
front: Why does a while loop freeze the game?
what: Each pass has to bring the condition closer to false, usually by changing a counter or taking something out of a list. If nothing changes, the loop never ends.
how:
while health > 0:
	health -= 10   # moves toward the end
example: Removing one item per pass from a list ends when the list is empty.
mistake: Putting the `+= 1` outside the loop, one tab too far left.

name: for loop
front: How do you repeat something a fixed number of times?
what: `for i in range(n)` runs the block n times, with `i` counting 0, 1, 2 … up to n minus 1.
example: `for i in range(4): move_forward(50)` draws four sides.
mistake: Expecting `range(3)` to reach 3. It stops at 2.

name: range()
front: What numbers does range(2, 6) give?
what: `range(n)` counts from 0 to n minus 1. `range(a, b)` counts from a up to b minus 1. `range(a, b, step)` jumps by step.
example: `for i in range(1, 4)` gives 1, 2, 3.
mistake: Counting the end value: it is never included.

name: Array
front: How do you keep several values in one variable?
what: An array is a list of values in order, written inside square brackets and separated by commas. It can be empty.
example: `var scores = [10, 20, 30]` holds three numbers.
mistake: Using round brackets: `(1, 2, 3)` is not an array.

name: size()
front: How many things are in an array?
what: `array.size()` gives the number of items. An empty array has size 0.
example: `if items.size() == 0:` checks for an empty inventory.
mistake: Writing `items.size` without brackets, or `len(items)`.

name: Arrays are shared
front: What happens when you assign an array to a second variable?
what: Both names point at the same array. Changing it through one name changes what the other sees. `duplicate()` makes a separate copy.
how:
var a = [1, 2]
var b = a
b.append(3)   # a is now [1, 2, 3] too
var c = a.duplicate()
example: Numbers and strings copy their value; arrays copy a reference.
mistake: Expecting `var b = a` to give b its own list.

name: for item in array
front: How do you do something with every item?
what: `for item in array` runs the block once per item, with `item` holding the current one each time.
example: Adding every score: `for score in scores: total += score`.
mistake: Changing `item` inside the loop and expecting the array to change. It is a copy of the value.

name: Looping with the position
front: How do you know which position you are at in a loop?
what: Loop over `range(array.size())` and use the counter as the index. `array[i]` is the item at that position.
how:
for i in range(items.size()):
	print(i, ": ", items[i])
example: Prints 0: bolt, 1: gear, 2: wire.
mistake: Looping to `items.size()` inclusive and reading one past the end.

name: String
front: How do you store text?
what: Text goes inside double quotes; that value is a String. It can hold letters, spaces, digits and be empty.
example: `"42"` is text; `42` is a number. They are different values.
mistake: Leaving off a quote: `"Robo` is an error on that line.

name: Joining strings
front: How do you put two pieces of text together?
what: `+` joins strings end to end. Nothing is added between them, so put the space in yourself.
how:
var line = "Hello " + name
var shout = name + "!"
example: `"Level " + str(level)` gives Level 3.
mistake: Adding a number to a string directly: `"Level " + 3` is an error; use `str(3)`.

name: str()
front: How do you turn a number into text?
what: `str(value)` gives the text form of any value, so it can be joined with other text.
example: `str(2.5)` is "2.5"; `str(true)` is "true".
mistake: Forgetting `str` and getting an error about String and int.

name: String methods
front: How do you get a string's length or change its case?
what: Strings have functions of their own, called with a dot: `length()`, `to_upper()`, `to_lower()`, `begins_with()`, `contains()`.
how:
var n = name.length()
var loud = name.to_upper()
example: `"robo".to_upper()` is "ROBO"; `"robo".length()` is 4.
mistake: Writing `length(name)` instead of `name.length()`.

name: return
front: How does a function give a value back?
what: `return` followed by a value ends the function and hands that value to whoever called it. The call itself then stands for the value.
example: `double(4)` is 8; `var d = double(4)` stores it.
mistake: Printing inside the function and returning nothing, then wondering why the caller gets null.

name: Using a returned value
front: What can you do with the result of a call?
what: Store it, print it, use it in a calculation, or pass it into another call. A call with a return value is an expression like any number.
example: `return add(a, b) + 1` uses the result straight away.
mistake: Calling the function and ignoring the result: `double(4)` alone does nothing visible.

name: return ends the function
front: What happens to the lines after return?
what: They never run. As soon as `return` runs the function is over, which also makes `return` a way to stop early.
example: With health 0 the function returns Down and never reaches the last line.
mistake: Putting the code you need after a return at the same level, so it is skipped every time.

name: append()
front: How do you add an item to the end of an array?
what: `array.append(value)` adds the value as the last item. The array grows by one.
example: Picking something up: `inventory.append(item)`.
mistake: Writing `items = items.append(x)`: append returns nothing, so items becomes null.

name: pop_back() and pop_front()
front: How do you take an item out of an array?
what: `pop_back()` removes and returns the last item; `pop_front()` the first. The array shrinks by one.
how:
var last = items.pop_back()
var first = items.pop_front()
example: Serving a queue: `var next = queue.pop_front()`.
mistake: Popping from an empty array, which gives null.

name: Index
front: How do you get the third item of an array?
what: Items are numbered from 0. `array[i]` is the item at position i, so the third item is `array[2]`.
how:
var items = ["bolt", "gear", "wire"]
print(items[0])   # bolt
print(items[2])   # wire
example: `scores[1]` is the second score.
mistake: Starting at 1. `items[3]` in a three-item array is past the end and crashes.

name: Counting from the end
front: How do you get the last item without knowing the size?
what: A negative index counts from the end: `array[-1]` is the last item, `array[-2]` the one before.
example: `items[-1]` on ["bolt", "gear", "wire"] is "wire".
mistake: Writing `items[items.size()]` for the last item: that is one past the end.

name: Changing an item by position
front: How do you replace one item in an array?
what: Assign to the position: `array[i] = value`. The array keeps its size; only that slot changes.
example: Healing the second robot: `healths[1] = 100`.
mistake: Assigning to a position that does not exist yet; use `append` to grow the array.

name: Dictionary
front: How do you look values up by name instead of by position?
what: A dictionary pairs keys with values inside curly brackets. You read a value by its key, not by a number.
example: `prices["bolt"]` gives the price of a bolt.
mistake: Using square brackets to create it, or forgetting the quotes around a text key.

name: Key and value
front: What are the two halves of a dictionary entry?
what: The key is the label you look up with; the value is what is stored under it. Keys are unique: one key, one value.
example: In `{"health": 100}` the key is "health" and the value 100.
mistake: Writing the same key twice and expecting both values to be kept.

name: Adding or changing an entry
front: How do you put a new entry in a dictionary?
what: Assign to the key: `dict[key] = value`. A new key is added; an existing key gets the new value.
example: `robot["level"] = 2` adds a level.
mistake: Using `append` on a dictionary: that is for arrays.

name: for key in dictionary
front: How do you loop over a dictionary?
what: `for key in dict` gives each key in turn; `dict[key]` inside the loop is the matching value.
how:
for name in prices:
	print(name, ": ", prices[name])
example: Prints bolt: 3, gear: 5 for `{"bolt": 3, "gear": 5}`.
mistake: Expecting the loop variable to be the value. It is the key.

name: keys() and values()
front: How do you get just the values of a dictionary?
what: `dict.keys()` gives an array of the keys, `dict.values()` an array of the values, in the same order.
how:
for amount in inventory.values():
	total += amount
example: `inventory.keys().size()` counts the entries.
mistake: Forgetting the brackets: `dict.values` is not the array.

name: int, float, String, bool
front: What kinds of value are there?
what: An int is a whole number, a float has a decimal point, a String is text in quotes, a bool is true or false. Each behaves a little differently.
how:
var count = 3        # int
var speed = 2.5      # float
var name = "Robo"    # String
var alive = true     # bool
example: `3` and `3.0` look alike but one is an int and one a float.
mistake: Comparing a number with text: `"3" == 3` is false.

name: Converting between types
front: How do you turn text into a number, or a number into text?
what: `int(x)`, `float(x)` and `str(x)` convert a value. `int()` drops the decimal part.
how:
var n = int("42")      # 42
var f = float(3)       # 3.0
var t = str(2.5)       # "2.5"
mistake: Expecting `int("7.5")` to work like float first. Convert to float, then int.

name: Type hint
front: What does `health: int` mean?
what: A type hint tells Godot which kind of value a variable or parameter holds. Godot then warns you when something else is put in. Hints are optional.
example: `var name: String = "Robo"` can only ever hold text.
mistake: Reading the colon as part of the name. The name is `health`; `int` is its type.

name: -> return type
front: What does `-> int` after a function mean?
what: It promises what kind of value the function returns. `-> void` means it returns nothing.
example: `-> bool` means the function answers true or false.
mistake: Writing `-> int` and then returning nothing on some path.

front: What does `var x := 5` mean?
what: `:=` declares the variable with a type worked out from the value: `5` makes it an int. It is a short way to write `var x: int = 5`.
how:
var count := 0        # int
var name := "Robo"    # String
example: `var speed := 2.5` is a float from then on.
mistake: Using `:=` with a value whose type Godot cannot tell yet, like a call that may return anything.
